title: Leveling the Playing Field -- Ch. 5: Protecting the Consumers
keywords: automobile, television and the personal computer
the right to safety, the right to be informed, the right to choose and the right to be heard
Tatad v. Secretary of the Department of Energy
Freedom from Debt Coalition v. ERC
Development Bank of the Philippines v. CA
Segovia Development Corp. v. Dumatol Realty
New Sampaguita Builders Construction v. Philippine National Bank
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' -- CJP's keynote address arguing that Supreme Court Decisions on the economy protect not only businessmen but consumers, who despite the century's great technological changes have 'remained at the center.'

Why Filipino consumers need protection: the lingering hold of caveat emptor, the preference for the cheaper unwarranted product, the cultural restraints of pakikisama and pakikipagkapwa, ignorance of legal remedies and the cost of suing, and a bargaining structure of standardized contracts dictated by the stronger party.

A survey of the Court's consumer jurisprudence across six fields -- constitutional policy favoring consumers, oil deregulation, public utility regulation and utility consumers, credit card transactions, adhesion contracts and interest rates under the Truth in Lending Act, and sales warranties and airline passengers.

The governing conclusion that 'the old adage caveat emptor no longer strictly applies to consumer transactions' -- on the contrary, 'the seller must equally beware,' and the Court 'will be ever ready to stand in the middle to protect the interests of consumers.'
sub_topics: He explains that he normally turns down speaking invitations but accepted the insistence of his compañero, former Comelec Commissioner Chino Marquinez, who argued the Court should discuss not only how its Decisions affected businessmen but how they protected consumers.

He opens with three phenomena of the twentieth century that changed social behavior: the automobile, which sent people upon the highroad; television, which did 'the opposite' by keeping them at home; and the personal computer with the Internet and cell phone, which let people work, shop and confer without leaving the house.

Amid trade liberalization, deregulation, globalization and privatization -- 'the third-millennium buzz words' -- and the blurring of national legal boundaries, concern for the consumer has grown more pronounced, resting on the rights to safety, to be informed, to choose and to be heard.

He quotes Lyndon B. Johnson on the consumer 'moving forward' and John F. Kennedy's 1962 message that consumers 'by definition include us all,' are the largest economic group, account for two-thirds of spending, and are 'the only important group in the economy who are not effectively organized.'

Four Filipino vulnerabilities: consumers still treat caveat emptor as controlling; they weigh a guaranteed product against a cheaper one sold 'as is' and, having 'taken the risk,' absorb the loss; they value pakikisama and pakikipagkapwa and sue only when a merchant is seen as walang kapwa-tao; and they lack awareness of rights and fear the cost of court battles against a powerful adversary.

The structural problem: consumer contracts are standardized and dictated by the stronger party, agents lack authority to adjust terms, and 'shopping around' is illusory where competitors offer essentially the same terms.

The Court's mandate: appellate review plus the power under Section 1 of Article VIII to set aside any act of any agency of government -- the Presidency and Congress included -- for grave abuse of discretion, meaning violation of the Constitution, law or doctrine, or whimsical and arbitrary action from manifest bias.

Tañada v. Angara: the Constitution favors consumers, not industries or enterprises; adherence to the WTO/GATT was upheld as aimed at the best goods and services at the most reasonable prices, affirming prosperity, employment, purchasing power and quality.

Oil deregulation: in Tatad v. Secretary of the Department of Energy the Court nullified RA 8180 not because it disagreed with deregulation as policy but because the law as 'cobbled by Congress' violated the Constitution -- 'more worthy of protection than the supra-normal profits of private corporations is the sanctity of the fundamental principles of the Constitution.'

He insists the Constitution makes the Court guardian of the people's economic as well as political rights: policy belongs to the President and Congress, but policies that fail the Constitution must be struck down 'not because they are unwise or inconvenient, but because they are constitutionally impermissible.'

Public utility regulation: rate regulation rests on police power; regulation must yield a fair return without prescribing rates so low as to deprive the utility of a reasonable return, 'a balancing of the investor and the consumer interests.'

Republic v. Meralco: income tax is not an operating expense, since customers derive no benefit from the taxes a utility pays, so the ERB's order that Meralco refund customers for amounts charged to cover its income tax liabilities was upheld.

Freedom from Debt Coalition v. ERC: a provisional rate increase transgressed the EPIRA law and its implementing rules, which require publication of the application in a local newspaper and consideration of the comments of customers and the local government unit -- procedural reforms that advance due process and 'people empowerment' and guard against provisional rates becoming 'virtually permanent.'

Spouses Quisumbing v. Meralco: a utility may not disconnect immediately without the requisites of law; consumers must be able to controvert an initial finding of illegal consumption, and failure to give prior written notice 'amounts to a tort' -- 'there is a right way to do the right thing at the right time for the right reason.'

Meralco v. Macrotextile Mills: where a defective meter was left uncorrected until the utility suddenly billed the unrecorded consumption, the company had to bear the loss, lest tolerance of delay encourage neglect by public utilities.

Credit cards: in BPI Express Card v. Olalia the consumer was not liable for purchases on an extension card he never applied for, adhesion contracts being construed strictly against the drafter; in Ermitaño v. C.A. prompt notice of loss sufficed, since a stipulation requiring the cardholder to wait for the company to notify member-establishments 'could clearly run against public policy'; and in Mandarin Villa v. CA the establishment that wrongfully dishonored an unexpired card was negligent -- its blame-the-customer argument 'so patently absurd that I need not even bother to answer it.'

Adhesion contracts and interest: obligations have the force of law and require mutuality, yet courts may reduce iniquitous penalties under Article 1229 -- as in Development Bank of the Philippines v. CA, where interest exceeded the principal, and Segovia Development Corp. v. Dumatol Realty, where a 3 percent monthly penalty meant 36 percent a year and the Court reduced rather than eliminated it, mindful that the seller remained unpaid.

Truth in Lending Act: in New Sampaguita Builders Construction v. Philippine National Bank, which he wrote, the Court struck down clauses letting lenders raise rates at their sole discretion without notice, held undisclosed charges uncollectible, and gave teeth to the forty-one-year-old statute.

Sales warranties: in Harrison Motors Corp. v. Nazario the seller's representation that taxes and duties had been paid was an express warranty under Article 1546; in Del Rosario v. CA the roofing seller acted in bad faith or gross negligence by withholding accessories and installing inferior materials contrary to its own brochures and advertisements.

Airline passengers: in Savellano v. Northwest Airlines the carrier could not unilaterally reroute passengers without consent, though only nominal damages were awarded absent proof of bad faith or of loss; in China Airlines v. Chiok, which he also wrote, the ticket-issuing airline is the principal and answers for the negligence of the endorsee-airline, and carriers were reminded to require rather than merely instruct their personnel to be accommodating.

stances.claim: Despite the automobile, television and the personal computer, the consumer has remained at the center of economic life, and the rights to safety, information, choice and a hearing have become priority concerns of nations and governments.
stances.rhetorical_move: historical sweep of three technological phenomena, then a pivot back to the constant

stances.claim: Filipino consumers are especially vulnerable, because caveat emptor still governs their thinking, cultural values like pakikisama discourage confrontation, they lack awareness of remedies, and standardized contracts leave them no bargaining power.
stances.rhetorical_move: enumerated cultural and structural diagnosis before the legal remedy

stances.claim: The Court may nullify an economic law such as the oil deregulation act not because it disagrees with the policy but because the statute as written offends the Constitution, whose sanctity outweighs the supra-normal profits of private corporations.
stances.rhetorical_move: separating policy wisdom from constitutional validity, then quoting the Decision

stances.claim: In a Third World country equal justice rings false unless economic rights, especially those of the poor, are protected as resolutely as liberty, so the Constitution makes the Court guardian of economic as well as political rights.
stances.rhetorical_move: equity appeal linking poverty to the meaning of equal justice

stances.claim: Caveat emptor no longer strictly applies: the seller must equally beware, and the Court will stand in the middle against fraudulent, unfair and iniquitous consumer practices.
stances.rhetorical_move: inversion of the classic maxim as the closing thesis

notable_anecdotes: He explains that he normally declines speaking invitations but yielded to the insistence of his compañero Chino Marquinez, who said the Court needed to show how its Decisions protected consumers and not only businessmen.

He sketches the twentieth century's turn from the automobile that 'sent people upon the highroad' to television that kept them home watching coronations, ball games, wars and moon landings, to the computer that let them shop and confer without leaving the house.
He recalls Kennedy's 1962 warning that if drugs are unsafe or prices exorbitant, the consumer's dollar is wasted, his health threatened, and the national interest suffers.

He recounts the Mandarin Villa establishment blaming the customer for not bringing enough cash after wrongfully dishonoring his unexpired card, dismissing the argument as a lame excuse too absurd to answer.

He notes the Court's declaration, 'probably for the first time,' that the forty-one-year-old Truth in Lending Act should be transformed from a paper tiger into a financial watchdog for hapless borrowers.
He describes the credit-card holder in Ermitaño who did everything the contract asked of her, only for the company to fail to warn its member-establishments in time.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Leveling the Playing Field' collects CJP's keynote address on how Supreme Court Decisions protect consumers, delivered after his compañero, former Comelec Commissioner Chino Marquinez, insisted the Court should explain its economic rulings from the consumer's side. He began with three phenomena that changed social behavior in the twentieth century -- the automobile, television and the personal computer -- and observed that through all of them the consumer had remained at the center, quoting Lyndon Johnson and John Kennedy's 1962 message that consumers include us all yet are the only important economic group not effectively organized. He then diagnosed four Filipino vulnerabilities: the hold of caveat emptor, the habit of buying the cheaper unwarranted good and absorbing the loss, the cultural restraints of pakikisama and pakikipagkapwa that delay legal action until a merchant is judged walang kapwa-tao, and ignorance of remedies coupled with the cost of suing, all aggravated by standardized contracts dictated by the stronger party. Against that background he surveyed the Court's consumer jurisprudence: Tañada v. Angara holding that the Constitution favors consumers rather than industries; Tatad v. Secretary of Energy striking down the oil deregulation law because the statute as cobbled by Congress offended the Constitution; Republic v. Meralco excluding income tax from operating expenses and ordering refunds; Freedom from Debt Coalition v. ERC voiding a provisional rate increase for want of publication and consultation; Quisumbing and Macrotextile on disconnection and utility delay; the credit-card cases of Olalia, Ermitaño and Mandarin Villa; DBP and Segovia on reducing iniquitous interest; and New Sampaguita Builders, which he wrote, giving teeth to the Truth in Lending Act by voiding undisclosed and unilaterally adjustable charges. He closed with sales-warranty and airline cases, including China Airlines v. Chiok, and the thesis that caveat emptor no longer strictly applies and that the seller must equally beware.
